cards.q: Which morphological operator has an effect that is most similar to convolution with an edge detection kernel?
method: An edge detection kernel outputs the boundaries of objects and gives nothing in flat areas.

A morphological gradient is the difference between a dilated or eroded image and another version of the image. The interior cancels out and only the outline is left. That is the same result as an edge detector.
Dilation, erosion, opening and closing all output filled shapes that are grown, shrunk or tidied. None of them outputs an outline.
cards.trap: Choosing Dilation or Erosion. Each one moves the boundary, but only a gradient isolates it.

cards.check: Blur kernels (mean, Gaussian) add up to 1 to keep brightness. Edge kernels add up to 0 to remove it.
cards.q: The coefficients in a linear edge detection kernel typically sum to what number?
method: In a flat area every pixel in the window has the same value v. The output is v × (sum of the coefficients).
An edge detector must give 0 where there is no edge, so the coefficients must add up to 0.
Test it on any edge kernel: Laplacian 4 − 1 − 1 − 1 − 1 = 0. Sobel 1 + 2 + 1 − 1 − 2 − 1 = 0.
cards.trap: Answering 1. That is the rule for blur kernels and the Sharpen kernel.

cards.check: Centre darker than the average of its four neighbours gives a negative answer. Centre brighter gives a positive answer. The answer must lie between −1020 and 1020.

working: Sign check: the centre (36) is darker than its neighbours (average about 83), so negative is expected.

cards.q: For the following 8-bit greyscale image matrix, calculate the output produced if a 3×3 Laplacian kernel defined below was applied centred at coordinate (2,2). Note that your answer will be ∈ ℤ, but will not necessarily be ∈ ℕ or ∈ [0..255].
method: Centre (2,2) is row 2, column 2. Find that pixel and its four direct neighbours: up, down, left, right.
Skip the four corners of the window. Their coefficients are 0.
Output = 4 × centre − (up + down + left + right).
The flip does not matter. The Laplacian kernel looks the same after a 180° turn. Enter the value with its sign.
cards.trap: Dropping the minus sign or entering 0. The question says the answer can be negative. Also do not subtract the corner pixels.

cards.check: The words "raw value, do not rescale" tell you the answer is above 255. The smallest possible output is 255 × (−8) = −2040.
cards.q: What is the maximum possible output of the following 2D Laplacian kernel for an 8-bit greyscale image? (note: provide the raw value; do not rescale).
method: Largest output = 255 × the sum of the positive coefficients. Put 255 under every positive coefficient and 0 under every negative one.
This kernel has one positive coefficient, +8, at the centre. Centre = 255 and all eight neighbours = 0.
The flip does not matter. The kernel looks the same after a 180° turn, and a turn never changes the sum of the positive coefficients.
cards.trap: Answering 255, or adding all the coefficients (8 − 8 = 0) and answering 0. Quiz 8 Question 14 has the same two mistakes.

cards.q: Which linear filter is sometimes applied prior to a Laplacian filter to reduce noise?
method: The Laplacian reacts to every fast change, so it makes noise stronger as well as edges.
A Gaussian blur first smooths the noise away. The two together are called the Laplacian of Gaussian.
Sobel and Prewitt are edge detectors, so they do not remove noise. Dilate is a morphological operator, not a linear filter.
cards.trap: Choosing Sobel or Prewitt because they belong to the same week. The question asks for a noise reducing filter, and that means a blur.

cards.check: The eight outputs always add up to 0, so the largest one is never negative. It can be at most 15 × 255 = 3825.

working: Best three in a row: 145 + 75 + 233 = 453 (the bottom row).

cards.q: For the following 8-bit greyscale image matrix, calculate the final (combined) output value that would be produced if the Kirsch compass kernel bank were applied. Formula: C(i,j) = max over z = 1..8 of E(z)(i,j).
method: Skip the centre pixel. Every Kirsch kernel has 0 at the centre. Add the eight outer pixels to get the ring total.
Each kernel has three 5s side by side on the ring and five −3s. Go round the ring and find the three neighbours in a row with the largest sum. The ring wraps round, so a triple can pass a corner.
Output = 8 × (best three) − 3 × (ring total). This works because 5 = 8 − 3.
The flip does not matter. Turning the whole bank through 180° gives the same eight kernels in a different order, so the largest output is the same.
cards.trap: Including the centre pixel (181 here) in a sum, or picking the three largest ring pixels when they are not next to each other.

cards.check: The answer is one of the two diagonal differences, so it is a whole number between 0 and 255.

working: With the kernels turned through 180°: Gx = 159 − 113 = 46.

cards.q: For the following 8-bit greyscale image matrix, calculate edge gradient Gxy if the 2×2 Robert's cross operator pair is applied. Use the formula max(|Gx|, |Gy|) to determine edge gradient. Round any answer ∈ ℝ/ℕ to be ∈ ℕ, and round .5 upwards. Formula: ∇I(x,y) = Gxy = max(|Gx|, |Gy|)
method: Each kernel uses one diagonal of the 2×2 image. Skip the two zero cells in each kernel.
Gx is the difference along the main diagonal (top-left and bottom-right). Gy is the difference along the other diagonal (top-right and bottom-left).
Take the absolute value of each and give the larger one.
The flip only changes the sign of Gx and Gy. The absolute value removes the sign, so the answer is the same with or without the flip.
cards.trap: Adding |Gx| and |Gy| (142 here) or using √(Gx² + Gy²). Read which formula the question gives. This one asks for the larger of the two.

cards.q: Which of the following is the most accurate method to calculate edge gradient (magnitude), given a pair of orthogonal filters, kx and ky, and outputs (Gx and Gy)? A. Absolute Sum: |Gx| + |Gy|. B. Absolute Max: max(|Gx|, |Gy|). C. Pythagorean: √(Gx² + Gy²).
method: Gx and Gy are two sides of a right-angled triangle. The true length of the gradient is the hypotenuse, √(Gx² + Gy²).
Absolute Sum and Absolute Max are quick estimates that avoid the square and the square root. Absolute Sum is too large and Absolute Max is too small for a diagonal edge.
Order for any numbers: Absolute Max ≤ Pythagorean ≤ Absolute Sum.
cards.trap: Choosing Absolute Sum because it uses both values. Accuracy and speed are different things. The two absolute formulas are faster, and Pythagorean is more accurate.

cards.check: The answer must be at least the larger of |Gx| and |Gy|, and at most |Gx| + |Gy|. Here it must be between 58 and 79.
cards.q: For the following 8-bit greyscale image matrix, calculate edge gradient Gxy if the 3×3 Prewitt operator pair is applied centred at coordinate (2,2). Using the Pythagorean formula, provided below, rather than |Gx| + |Gy| or max(|Gx|, |Gy|). Round any answer ∈ ℝ/ℕ to be ∈ ℕ, and round .5 upwards. Formula: ∇I(x,y) = Gxy = √(Gx² + Gy²)
method: kx has a zero middle column, so skip it. Gx = (sum of the left column) − (sum of the right column).
ky has a zero middle row, so skip it. Gy = (sum of the top row) − (sum of the bottom row).
Gxy = √(Gx² + Gy²). Round at the end.
The flip only changes the sign of Gx and Gy (right − left and bottom − top). Squaring removes the sign, so the answer is the same with or without the flip.
cards.trap: Including the centre pixel (237 here). Both kernels have 0 at the centre. Also do not round Gx or Gy part way through.

cards.check: The angle is between −90° and 90°. It is positive when Gx and Gy have the same sign. It is below 45° in size when |Gy| is smaller than |Gx|. An answer below 1.6 in size means the calculator is in radians.
cards.q: For the following 8-bit greyscale image matrix, calculate the gradient direction (angle) if the 3×3 Sobel operator pair is applied centred at coordinate (2,2). Express you answer in degrees (not radians). Write you answer to 2 d.p. Formula: θ = arctan(Gy ÷ Gx)
method: Same column and row sums as Question 9, but Sobel counts the middle pixel of each column or row twice (weights 1, 2, 1). Skip the zero middle column for Gx and the zero middle row for Gy.
Gx = weighted left column − weighted right column. Gy = weighted top row − weighted bottom row.
θ = arctan(Gy ÷ Gx) with the calculator in degrees. Gy goes on top. Keep the signs of Gx and Gy when dividing.
The flip changes the sign of both Gx and Gy. The two minus signs cancel in the division, so the angle is the same with or without the flip.
cards.trap: Leaving the calculator in radians (0.44 here), dividing Gx by Gy, or forgetting the weight of 2. Also rounding the division first. arctan(0.4732) gives 25.32, but the exact value 25.3251 rounds to 25.33. Keep the full value on the calculator and round once at the end.

cards.check: Three plots are slopes and one is a spike. The spike is the Laplacian.
cards.q: Match the following edge detection filter surface plots to the corresponding filter names.
cards.ans: A → Robert's Cross. B → Laplacian. C → Sobel. D → Prewitt.
method: Find the Laplacian first. It is the only one that is the same in every direction: one sharp spike in the middle with a dip around it.
Robert's Cross is a 2×2 kernel, so its mesh is coarse. It shows one hump and one dip across the diagonal.

Sobel and Prewitt are both slopes, high on one side and low on the other. Prewitt has weights 1, 1, 1, so it is a plain ramp, level along its length. Sobel has weights 1, 2, 1, so its ridge and valley bulge in the middle.
cards.trap: Swapping Sobel and Prewitt. Look along the high edge: level means Prewitt, humped in the middle means Sobel.

cards.q: What is the current de facto approach for effective edge detection?
method: De facto means the method people use in practice as the standard.
Canny is a full algorithm, not one kernel. It blurs with a Gaussian, finds the gradient, thins the edges and then applies hysteresis thresholding. This gives thin, clean edges with little noise.
Sobel is the tempting wrong option. It is common, but it is only one step, and Canny gives better results.
cards.trap: Choosing Sobel because it is the kernel pair used most in the calculations.

cards.check: Work out one corner in full. With the window at the top-left, the 1 is in the bottom-right cell of the window. Cross correlation uses the kernel as printed, so the 9 sits on the 1 and the top-left output is 9. Convolution uses the turned kernel, so the 1 sits on the 1 and the top-left output is 1. All nine kernel numbers appear once in each output, and the centre is 5 in both.

working: Check the top-left cell. The window covers rows 1 to 3 and columns 1 to 3, and the 1 is in the bottom-right cell of the window.
Cross correlation, kernel as printed: the 9 sits on the 1. Top-left output = 9.
Convolution, kernel turned to 9 8 7 / 6 5 4 / 3 2 1: the 1 sits on the 1. Top-left output = 1.

cards.q: It was mentioned that we horizontally and vertically flip a kernel before using it when we perform 2D convolution, but forego these flip operations when performing cross correlation (which is otherwise an identical procedure). To illustrate the implications of the flip operations, perform convolution and cross correlation on the following image matrix. Use the "valid convolution" approach at the image boundaries. Enter the 3×3 output with cross correlation and the 3×3 output with convolution.
cards.ans: Output with Cross Correlation: 9 8 7 / 6 5 4 / 3 2 1 (the kernel turned through 180°). Output with Convolution: 1 2 3 / 4 5 6 / 7 8 9 (the kernel as printed).
method: Valid means the kernel must fit fully inside the image. A 5×5 image and a 3×3 kernel give a 3×3 output, one value for each of the nine window positions.
The image is a single 1 at the centre, on zeros. For that image no multiplication is needed. Each output is a copy of the kernel.
Convolution output: write the kernel as printed, 1 2 3 / 4 5 6 / 7 8 9.
Cross correlation output: write the kernel turned through 180°, 9 8 7 / 6 5 4 / 3 2 1.
The two outputs differ because the kernel 1 to 9 has no symmetry. A symmetric kernel would give the same output twice.
cards.trap: Entering 5 in the centre and 0 everywhere else for both outputs. The 1 is inside all nine windows, so no output cell is 0. The other common mistake is swapping the two outputs. Convolution copies the kernel and cross correlation turns it.

cards.check: The centre cell of each output uses the whole 1 to 9 block. Cross correlation centre = 1² + 2² + ... + 9² = 285. Convolution centre = 1×9 + 2×8 + ... + 9×1 = 165. In the cross correlation output every corner and edge cell must be smaller than 285, because those windows hold fewer non-zero pixels.

working: Top-left window (rows 1 to 3, columns 1 to 3) is 0 0 0 / 0 1 2 / 0 4 5.
Centre window is 1 2 3 / 4 5 6 / 7 8 9. Cross correlation = 285. Convolution = 165.
Cross correlation, five cells worked out: top row 94, 154, 106, middle-left 186, centre 285. The other four are copies.
Convolution, all nine cells worked out: 26 56 54 / 84 165 144 / 134 236 186.

cards.q: It was mentioned that we horizontally and vertically flip a kernel before using it when we perform 2D convolution, but forego these flip operations when performing cross correlation (which is otherwise an identical procedure). To illustrate the implications of the flip operations, perform convolution and cross correlation on the following image matrix. Use the "valid convolution" approach at the image boundaries. Enter the 3×3 output with cross correlation and the 3×3 output with convolution.
cards.ans: Output with Cross Correlation: 94 154 106 / 186 285 186 / 106 154 94. Output with Convolution: 26 56 54 / 84 165 144 / 134 236 186.
method: Valid gives a 3×3 output. Each output cell is one whole window. Multiply the matching pairs and add them into a single number.
Skip the zero border cells of the image. A corner window has only four non-zero pixels. An edge window has six. Only the centre window uses all nine.
Cross correlation: use the kernel as printed, 1 2 3 / 4 5 6 / 7 8 9. Work out five cells only: the top row, the middle-left cell and the centre.

Copy those values through the centre to fill the other four cells. Top-left goes to bottom-right, top-middle to bottom-middle, top-right to bottom-left and middle-left to middle-right. The copy works because the image block and the kernel hold the same numbers.
Convolution: first write the kernel turned through 180°, 9 8 7 / 6 5 4 / 3 2 1. Then work out all nine windows with it. The convolution output has no such pattern, so no cell can be copied.
cards.trap: Entering the nine separate products of the centre window (1, 4, 9, ... 81 for cross correlation and 9, 16, 21, ... 9 for convolution). Add those nine products together. The sum fills only the centre cell (285 and 165). The other eight cells come from moving the window.

cards.check: The answer is never negative. It is at least (largest difference)² ÷ 9, which is 22500 ÷ 9 = 2500 here. It cannot be above 255² = 65025. For a second route, enter the nine differences as data in the calculator's statistics mode and read Σx². Σx² must equal the sum of the squares, 54541 here.
cards.q: Given an image patch, L, and a template of an object we are seeking, t, one way to measure their degree of similarity is to calculate MSE (Mean Square Error), where in this case w is the width of our 2D symmetric template. Give your answer to 2 d.p. Formula: MSE(L,t) = (1 ÷ w²) × Σᵢ Σⱼ (L(i,j) − t(i,j))², with i and j from 1 to w.
method: Pair each cell of L with the cell of t in the same place. There is no kernel and no flip.
For each pair, take the larger value minus the smaller. Write the nine differences. The sign can be dropped because every difference is squared next.
Type the nine squares into the calculator as one sum, such as 41² + 24² + ..., and press =.
Divide the sum by w² = 9. Round to 2 decimal places.
cards.trap: Adding the differences before squaring, so negatives cancel. Also dividing by w = 3 instead of w² = 9. Write the answer as 6060.11, with no thousands comma.
